---
title: "Evaluation Speed"
subtitle: "Every strength result in this project compares engines at matched search depth. At matched *time*, GNU Backgammon is ahead — by a margin that decides what the engine can do."
toc-depth: 2
jupyter: python3
---

Raccoon's network is more accurate than GNU Backgammon's, position for position.
On the BGSage benchmark it selects moves better at 0-ply than GNU Backgammon does
at 1-ply. That result is real and it is measured.

It is also bought with about three and a half thousand times the computation, and
that has never been reported alongside it.

This page measures what one position evaluation costs each engine, checks whether
the difference is the implementation or the network, and works out what it means
for the searches both engines can afford. The conclusion is that the current
architecture cannot be made practical by tuning, and that the choice recorded in
`goal.md`'s first assumption is the thing to revisit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

S = json.loads(
    (Path("../experiments/exp027-speed-audit/results/eval_speed.json")).read_text()
)
R, G, RATIO = S["raccoon"], S["gnubg"], S["ratios"]
```

## What one position costs

Both figures below come from the same script on the same machine in the same run,
so the ratio does not depend on comparing published numbers from different
hardware.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| engine | architecture | MACs / position | positions / second |")
print("|---|---|---:|---:|")
print(f"| GNU Backgammon | {G['architecture']} | {G['macs_per_position']/1e6:.3f} M | "
      f"**{G['boards_per_second']:,.0f}** |")
print(f"| Raccoon ep22 | {R['architecture']}, {R['parameters']/1e6:.1f} M parameters | "
      f"{R['macs_per_position']/1e6:.0f} M | **{R['boards_per_second_best']:,.0f}** |")
print()
print(f": Measured on {S['machine']['node']}, {S['machine']['cpu_count']} cores. "
      f"MACs are multiply-accumulates in one forward pass, computed from the "
      f"network shape.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"GNU Backgammon evaluates **{RATIO['throughput_gnubg_over_raccoon']:,.0f} "
      f"times** as many positions per second, while Raccoon does "
      f"**{RATIO['macs_raccoon_over_gnubg']:,.0f} times** the multiply-accumulates "
      f"per position.")
```

## It is the network, not the code

The two ratios differ, and the direction is worth noting: the arithmetic gap is
larger than the measured gap. Raccoon extracts more work per multiply-accumulate
than GNU Backgammon does, because a convolutional network evaluated in batches
uses wide vector instructions and several cores, while a small network evaluated
one position at a time does not.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
eff = RATIO["macs_raccoon_over_gnubg"] / RATIO["throughput_gnubg_over_raccoon"]
print(f"Raccoon reaches **{R['gflops_achieved']:.0f} GFLOPS**, against a "
      f"theoretical peak near 410 for this processor — about "
      f"{R['gflops_achieved']/410:.0%} of it, which is good for convolutions on a "
      f"2x12 board. Its advantage in efficiency per operation is {eff:.1f}x; its "
      f"arithmetic disadvantage is {RATIO['macs_raccoon_over_gnubg']:,.0f}x.")
```

So there is no implementation problem to fix. Quantisation, better kernels or a
faster runtime might buy a factor of two or three. The gap is three to four
orders of magnitude, and it is the shape of the network.

## What it costs at matched time

Search cost is evaluation cost multiplied by tree size. Two engines searching to
the same depth visit comparable numbers of positions, so a per-position gap of
this size becomes a per-decision gap of the same size.

Putting the measured per-decision times next to the benchmark accuracy each
configuration achieves:

| configuration | time / decision | benchmark PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| GNU Backgammon, 2-ply | 0.062 s | **0.588** |
| Raccoon, 0-ply | 0.049 s | 1.026 |
| Raccoon, depth-2 expectimax | 28 s | 0.426 |

The first two lines take about the same time, and GNU Backgammon wins. The third
line is the configuration where Raccoon is clearly stronger, and it costs roughly
450 times as long as the opponent it beats.

Times are measured: GNU Backgammon's from driving the binary
(`raccoon/eval/gnubg_cli.py`), Raccoon's 0-ply from the throughput above at about
21 evaluations per decision, and depth-2 from exp021's recorded 12,016
evaluations per decision. PR figures are exp021's, on a 2,000-decision sample.

**Every comparison this project has published is at matched depth.** exp021's
ladder, exp026's head-to-head, the benchmark tables: all of them hold search depth
fixed and vary the engine. None holds *time* fixed. At matched time the ordering
reverses, and that is the comparison a real game imposes.

## Everyone else uses a small network

| engine | network |
|---|---|
| TD-Gammon | one hidden layer, handcrafted inputs |
| GNU Backgammon | 250 → 128 → 5, one per position class |
| BGSage (measured close to eXtreme Gammon) | 244 → 200/400 → 5, five to nineteen networks by game plan |
| Raccoon | 26-channel input, ten residual blocks at 256 channels |

The convolutional trunk came from the AlphaZero framing in `goal.md`. Convolutions
assume neighbouring squares are related in a way worth exploiting with shared
filters. A backgammon board is 24 points where the relationships that matter are
pip distances, contact and blot exposure — quantities Raccoon's encoder already
computes and hands the network directly as channels 17 to 25. It is possible that
285 M multiply-accumulates are being spent partly to rediscover structure the
input already contains.

## What a smaller network would cost

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| architecture | MACs / position | projected positions / second | speed-up |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|")
base = R["boards_per_second_best"]
for row in S["projected_architectures"]:
    print(f"| {row['name']} | {row['macs_per_position']/1e6:.3f} M | "
          f"{row['projected_boards_per_second']:,.0f} | "
          f"{row['projected_boards_per_second']/base:,.0f}x |")
```

These rows scale the measured throughput by arithmetic cost. **They say what an
architecture would cost, not what it would score.** A cheaper network is only
useful if it stays accurate enough, and that requires training one and measuring
it.

The measurement worth making is accuracy against speed, not accuracy alone. exp017
established that scaling from 8 M to 40 M training positions took PR from 2.16 to
0.93 at the current size, and the size itself was never varied against the same
data. The 40 M-position cache is on disk and `scripts/train_distill.py` already
does the work, so distilling it into progressively smaller networks — including a
plain network over the existing handcrafted features — is a matter of compute
rather than new machinery.

A cheaper network reaching, say, PR 1.2 at forty times the speed would beat ep22
outright at equal time, because it could afford the depth-2 search ep22 cannot.

## exp028: a small network, measured {#exp028}

The page above argued that the experiment worth running was accuracy against
speed, not accuracy alone. This is that experiment.

```{python}
#| echo: false
E = json.loads(
    (Path("../experiments/exp028-mlp/results/exp028_summary.json")).read_text()
)
P, REF, ARMS, PAIR = E["protocol"], E["reference_points"], E["arms"], E["paired"]
```

**Protocol**, fixed before the final arms and not varied: every score is the full
BGSage benchmark, `{python} f"n = {P['n']:,}"`, with no subsampling anywhere;
every comparison is paired on identical decisions and bootstrapped over the 500
generating games; the paired resolution is about
`{python} f"{P['resolution_pr']}"` PR, and effects below it are reported as *not
resolved*, which is not the same as a null. Training data is the same 43 M GNU
Backgammon 2-ply labels ep22 was distilled from.

### The architecture, and what the inputs cost

Distilling those labels into a network shaped after PureTD's
`[512, 512, 256, 256]` gives a curve that is monotone in capacity:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = [("MLP [256], 624 inputs", 5.4), ("MLP [256,256], 624 inputs", 2.99),
        ("MLP [512,512], 624 inputs", 2.31),
        ("MLP [512,512,256,256], 624 inputs", 1.93),
        ("...dropping the handcrafted channels, 408 inputs", 1.74),
        ("...de-broadcast to 201 inputs", 1.68)]
print("| configuration | PR |")
print("|---|---:|")
for label, pr in rows:
    print(f"| {label} | {pr:.2f} |")
print()
print(": Every row is the full benchmark. These arms ran under a constant "
      "learning rate, later shown to leave about 0.2 PR unclaimed, so they order "
      "the configurations correctly but none of them is converged.")
```

Two input results are worth separating. Dropping the nine handcrafted channels
*improved* PR by 0.19 while removing compute — confirming PureTD's claim that
expert features are unnecessary. But the mechanism is duplication rather than the
features themselves: channels 8 to 25 are all constant across the board, so a
convolution receives them as planes and a flattened network receives 24 identical
copies of each. De-broadcasting to one value per scalar channel gives 201 inputs,
which is the size PureTD uses, and buys another 0.10.

More data bought nothing: 24 M to 43 M positions moved PR by 0.04, inside the
noise. That measurement was made under the constant-LR schedule, so it is worth
repeating rather than treating as settled.

### Two hypotheses, tested

With capacity, inputs and data explored, two candidates remained. Four arms,
identical but for one variable each, all at the same 20-epoch budget:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
labels = {"ref20": "reference (constant LR, six-outcome head)",
          "scalar20": "scalar head, squared error on equity",
          "cosine20": "cosine learning-rate decay",
          "combined20": "both"}
keys = {"scalar20": "scalar_vs_outcomes6", "cosine20": "cosine_vs_constant_lr",
        "combined20": "combined_vs_reference"}
print("| arm | PR at epoch 20 | paired vs reference | |")
print("|---|---:|---:|:--|")
for a in ("ref20", "scalar20", "cosine20", "combined20"):
    pr = ARMS[a]["pr_final"]
    if a == "ref20":
        print(f"| {labels[a]} | {pr:.3f} | — | |")
    else:
        d = PAIR[keys[a]]
        print(f"| {labels[a]} | **{pr:.3f}** | {d['gain']:+.3f} "
              f"[{d['ci95'][0]:+.3f}, {d['ci95'][1]:+.3f}] | {d['verdict']} |")
```

**Both hypotheses are confirmed**, each worth about 0.2 PR. The learning rate had
been fixed at 1e-3 for the whole of every previous run, and the training target
had been cross-entropy over six outcomes rather than squared error on the
quantity move selection actually ranks.

**They do not add.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
A = E["additivity"]
cvc, cvs = PAIR["combined_vs_cosine"], PAIR["combined_vs_scalar"]
print(f"Independent effects would have given "
      f"{A['predicted_if_independent']:.3f}; the combined arm reached "
      f"**{A['observed']:.3f}**. That prediction was written into the run script "
      f"before the arm started. Against cosine alone the combination is "
      f"{cvc['gain']:+.3f} [{cvc['ci95'][0]:+.3f}, {cvc['ci95'][1]:+.3f}] — "
      f"*{cvc['verdict']}* — while against the scalar head alone it is "
      f"{cvs['gain']:+.3f} [{cvs['ci95'][0]:+.3f}, {cvs['ci95'][1]:+.3f}], "
      f"*{cvs['verdict']}*. So the schedule does most of the work and the two "
      f"were largely repairing the same deficiency.")
```

### Convergence had to be measured, repeatedly

The reference arm was **still improving at epoch 20**: each five-epoch step was
individually below the resolution limit, but epochs 10 to 20 accumulate to a real
gain.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| arm | epochs 10 → 20 | |")
print("|---|---:|:--|")
for a in ("ref20", "scalar20", "cosine20", "combined20"):
    d = PAIR[f"{a}_e10_to_e20"]
    print(f"| {labels[a]} | {d['gain']:+.3f} "
          f"[{d['ci95'][0]:+.3f}, {d['ci95'][1]:+.3f}] | {d['verdict']} |")
```

This is why the protocol above insists convergence is measured rather than
inferred. Training loss cannot see it — the reference network and a far weaker one
produce indistinguishable loss curves. Nor can adjacent epoch comparisons, which
read *not resolved* three times in a row on a curve that was genuinely still
descending. Only the longer interval showed it.

### Where it leaves the architecture

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
best = ARMS["combined20"]["pr_final"]
print("| engine | value MACs | PR |")
print("|---|---:|---:|")
print(f"| PureTD (see note) | {REF['puretd']['macs']/1e6:.3f} M | {REF['puretd']['pr']:.2f} |")
print(f"| Raccoon ep22, ResNet 10x256 | {REF['ep22_resnet_10x256']['macs']/1e6:.0f} M | "
      f"{REF['ep22_resnet_10x256']['pr']:.3f} |")
print(f"| GNU Backgammon, 1-ply | — | {REF['gnubg_1ply']['pr']:.3f} |")
print(f"| **This MLP, best configuration** | **{0.563:.3f} M** | **{best:.3f}** |")
print(f"| GNU Backgammon, 0-ply | {REF['gnubg_0ply']['macs']/1e6:.3f} M | "
      f"{REF['gnubg_0ply']['pr']:.2f} |")
```

A network doing **500 times less arithmetic than ep22** reaches PR
`{python} f"{ARMS['combined20']['pr_final']:.3f}"`, against ep22's 0.950. It beats
GNU Backgammon's own evaluator comfortably and still loses to GNU Backgammon at
1-ply.

**On the PureTD comparison, two qualifications.** Their 0.94 is XG++ Performance
Rating on *cubeful* money; ours is this benchmark's PR on *cubeless checker play*.
The two scales agree closely where they can be compared — GNU Backgammon at 0-ply
is 2.18 on theirs and 2.14 on ours, at 1-ply 1.21 against 1.206 — which is why
they are shown together, but they are not the same measurement. And while
**capacity and inference cost are matched** (562 k parameters against 565 k, 0.561 M
MACs against 0.563 M), **training compute is not**: 200 M self-play games over
about 65 hours on a 64-core workstation with a GPU, against roughly 38 core-hours
per arm here with no GPU. Two orders of magnitude.

That distinction decides what to try next. The remaining difference is either the
**method** — on-policy TD with exact Bellman backups over all 21 rolls, rather
than regressing a fixed teacher — or simply **scale**. The evidence against pure
scale is that more data bought nothing, but that was measured under the broken
schedule. Running the best configuration far longer separates the two for one
arm's cost, before committing to an RL pipeline that would take weeks.

## What this page does not say

* **It does not say the network is bad.** It is more accurate per position than
  GNU Backgammon's by a wide margin. The question is the price.
* **The projected rows above are arithmetic, not accuracy.** exp028 measured the
  accuracy separately; see [that section](#exp028).
* **exp028's arms are compared at a fixed budget, not at their endpoints.** The
  cosine arm is converged by construction, since its learning rate reaches zero;
  the constant-rate arm was still improving when it stopped. "Better at 20 epochs"
  is a weaker claim than "reaches a better endpoint".
* **It is one machine.** A four-core desktop processor with no GPU. A graphics
  card changes Raccoon's throughput far more than GNU Backgammon's, because
  batched convolutions suit one and a per-position network does not. That changes
  the arithmetic for training and offline analysis; it does not change what a
  browser or a phone can run.
* **GNU Backgammon's figure is single-position and single-threaded.** It has
  headroom of its own that this comparison does not give it.
* **It retracts no published result.** Raccoon does beat GNU Backgammon at matched
  depth on the benchmark. This page adds the axis those results were silent on.
